doc.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013

title: Coltrane, Ayler and the Lester Young tradition; Dexter Gordon
summary: He admired Coltrane but stayed in the Lester Young tradition, loved Dexter Gordon's records, and in Copenhagen found Dexter, Ben Webster and Kenny Drew at Montmartre.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Were you hearing Coltrane and the sort of avante garde, well sort of progressive stuff that was going on in the sixties? Were you hearing it and listening to it?

I was listening to it. I admired Coltrane. I thought it was absolutely fantastic. But I didn’t want to copy him because it was so unique and I didn’t want to make a pale image of what Coltrane was doing. A lot of what he was doing was beyond my understanding at that point. And I had needed to just sit down and listen to him. I was also familiar with Albert Ayler, who was just ripping and tearing. But I was more back in the tradition. I was kind of steeped in the Lester Young style of playing. And one of my favorite tenor players was Dexter Gordon, who was just terrific. I mean I had a ton of his albums. And I used to like the kind of sarcastic way that he played [scats]. He would do that. And you would hear these little phrases on all of his recordings. But he could interpret a ballad like nobody’s business. And so after being in France and then kind of working my way up through Europe, I wound up in Copenhagen and guess who’s on the schedule for Montmartre? Dexter. And also I scout around and Webster was also playing there at the time, Sahib Shihab was playing there, Kenny Drew was playing there, and there were so many wonderful bass players there.
